text: You're a child of light. You may do something dark, but you never become darkness.
explanation:
"You are all sons of light and sons of the day. We are not of the night nor of darkness." Some teaching leaves believers feeling that they slip in and out of the light many times a day. But a prince can do a pauper's work and still be a prince; a man can act like a monkey and he's still a man.

Sin is never good for you, but it doesn't change what you are. If you've been born again, you are a son or daughter of the day, and that's a settled identity, not a daily verdict.

text: When thick darkness covered Egypt for three days, "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."
explanation:
The darkness was so thick that the Egyptians couldn't see one another or move from their places. Notice: if Israel's light had come from lamps or candles, the Egyptians could have lit theirs too. It was a supernatural light, a gift of grace, given only to God's people.

Isaiah 60 says that in the last days darkness will cover the earth, but the Lord will arise over you. Whatever darkness covers the world, your nation or your street, God's people can have light in their homes and families.

text: Walking in the light is where you are, not how well you're doing. That's why the blood is still cleansing you there.
explanation:
"If we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin." It doesn't say "according to the light," as though it were measured by your obedience. No one could walk according to the light God has. It's about location.

And if walking in the light meant not sinning, why would the blood need to keep cleansing us there? When a believer has a bad thought or says a wrong word, they don't drop into darkness and have to climb back. They're in the light, and the blood keeps them clean.

text: Jesus said His followers "shall not walk in darkness," a double negative in Greek: certainly never.
explanation:
"I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life." The Greek "ou me" is the strongest possible negative: no way, never. It's used sparingly, in places like "I will never leave you" and "blessed is the man to whom the Lord shall not impute sin."

The same John later writes about someone who hates his brother and walks in darkness. He's describing someone who claims to be in the light but isn't; as he says, "they went out from us, but they were not of us." For the one who truly follows Jesus, darkness is not your address.

text: God said "Let there be light" on day one. The sun wasn't made until day four.
explanation:
The first time Scripture records God speaking, He says, "Let there be light." But the sun, moon and stars came on the fourth day. So what was that first light? In Hebrew, "let there be" (yehi) begins with yod and hey, the first two letters of God's covenant name, a hint that the light is from Himself.

Jesus is the light of the world, the light that was there before the sun. Things often look darker at night; worries and sickness feel heavier after sunset. But you're not a child of the night. Your light doesn't depend on circumstances; it's a Person.

text: The Holy Spirit is God's down payment, His guarantee that He's coming back for all of you, body included.
explanation:
You were "sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the guarantee of our inheritance." The Greek word means a deposit: in the ancient marketplace, if you bought something too big to carry, you paid a deposit as a pledge that you'd return to collect it.

The one blessing no believer can have yet is the new body: immortal, never tired, never sick, never ageing, like Jesus' risen body that could be touched and could eat fish. Until then we trust God for health and strength. And the Spirit inside you is His promise that the full redemption is coming.

text: The Jews sought light, the Greeks sought knowledge, the Romans sought glory. All three shine in the face of Jesus Christ.
explanation:
"God who commanded light to shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." In Paul's day the Jews looked for light and revelation, the Greeks pursued wisdom and philosophy, and the Romans chased military and imperial glory.

People today still chase the same three: mystical enlightenment, education and knowledge, and fame or wealth. Paul says every one of them is found in one place: the face of Jesus. Put Him at the centre of your life, your marriage and your parenting, and you'll find what everyone else is looking for.
